subject: 'Structuring' seizures under the Bank Secrecy Act — the IRS's 2013 seizure of Carole Hinders's cash-only restaurant bank account (~$33,000) with no criminal charge, and the October 2014 IRS policy reversal.
central_question: Can the IRS empty your bank account simply because you deposited your own cash in amounts under $10,000 — even if you broke no other law?
viewer_promise: By the end, the viewer understands what 'structuring' is, how a cash-only restaurant owner of nearly 40 years lost her entire bank account without ever being charged, and how public outrage forced the IRS to change the rule and return the money.
surprise: Carole Hinders ran a small cash-only Mexican restaurant in Iowa for about 38 years and regularly deposited less than $10,000 at a time — the exact amount that triggers a mandatory bank report. The IRS treated that pattern itself as the crime ('structuring') and seized about $33,000 from her account. No charges were filed. Following the bank's own reporting threshold was treated as the offense.
stakes: How anti-money-laundering rules built for drug cartels swept up ordinary cash businesses; the seize-first, charge-never pattern; and the 2014 policy change that reined it in.
target_audience: English-speaking US general audience; small-business owners, anyone paid in cash, and anyone with a bank account; relatable and almost entirely unknown to the public.
demand_evidence: 'Why did the bank report my deposit' / 'structuring law' is a real, anxious everyday-money query; this case is the human, extreme version.
Extends the channel's proven second-person threat vein to money in the bank; reframes dry financial regulation as a personal risk.
A sympathetic 38-year small-business owner and an absurd trigger ('I followed the rule and lost everything') — high curiosity gap, low competition.
competition: The structuring seizures got a burst of 2014-2015 news coverage, then faded; few explainers tell the Hinders story cleanly and tie it to the rule change, sourced and neutral.
differentiation: A true-story-forward small-business-and-bank episode (distinct visual lane from EP33's home and EP34's airport): one sympathetic owner, an absurd $10,000 threshold, and a real policy reversal as the payoff, sourced to contemporaneous reporting and the Institute for Justice record. Closing chapter of the three-part 'they took everything' arc.
research_feasibility: High: contemporaneous coverage (New York Times, 2014), Institute for Justice case materials (Hinders; the parallel Lyndon McLellan case), the IRS's October 2014 policy statement limiting structuring seizures, the Bank Secrecy Act structuring statute (31 U.S.C. Section 5324) and 2015 congressional hearings.
visual_feasibility: High: a small family restaurant and cash register; the $10,000 bank-report threshold as a diagram; a plain-language 'structuring' explainer; a frozen/seized account; a timeline from seizure (2013) to the IRS reversal (Oct 2014) and the return of the money. No real-person likeness; all illustration.
risk_notes: Real, named private individual (Carole Hinders) as a sympathetic protagonist: describe strictly and accurately per the public record and reporting; NO real-person likeness (invariant 11).
No criminal charges were filed and the money was ultimately returned; state this clearly and do not imply wrongdoing.
Describe the IRS factually and neutrally; note the agency changed its policy in October 2014 — this is a systemic-rule story, not an accusation against individuals.
Amount seized was the restaurant's business bank account (about $33,000); describe precisely and avoid overstating it as her total net worth.
Generated visuals are illustration/reconstruction, never presented as authentic footage.
kill_conditions: Cannot source the seizure, the absence of charges, and the 2014 IRS policy reversal to contemporaneous reporting plus the Institute for Justice record.
